subject: art-design
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which three colours are the primary colours in painting?
questions.explain: The painting primaries are red, yellow and blue, from which the secondary colours are mixed.

questions.q: How does cross-hatching create tone in a drawing?
options: By layering sets of intersecting parallel lines
By rubbing colour with a finger to blend it
By applying thick dabs of paint
By scratching into a painted surface
questions.explain: Cross-hatching builds up tone through overlapping sets of parallel lines drawn at angles to one another.

questions.q: Adding white to a colour produces a...
questions.explain: A tint is a colour lightened with white, whereas a shade is a colour darkened with black.

questions.q: What does the term 'chiaroscuro' describe?
options: The strong contrast between light and dark to model form
questions.explain: Chiaroscuro is the use of marked light and dark contrast to give figures and objects a sense of three-dimensional form.

questions.q: Impasto is a painting technique in which...
options: Paint is applied thickly so that brush or knife marks are visible
Paint is heavily diluted to create transparent washes
Colour is scratched away to reveal layers beneath
Dots of pure colour are placed side by side
questions.explain: Impasto involves laying paint on thickly so the texture of the strokes and the medium itself stands out from the surface.

questions.q: A student wants a smooth, gradual transition from dark to light in a graphite drawing. Which approach is most suitable?
options: Blending the graphite gradually with a stump or finger
Bold stippling with widely spaced dots
Applying paint thickly with a palette knife
Scratching marks into the paper surface
questions.explain: Blending softens and merges tones, producing the smooth continuous gradation the student is aiming for.

questions.q: What is the effect of placing complementary colours next to one another?
options: Each colour appears more intense and vibrant
Both colours appear duller and greyer
The result is a monochromatic effect
The colours automatically blend into a tint
questions.explain: Complementary colours sit opposite on the colour wheel and, placed side by side, heighten each other's intensity through contrast.

questions.q: Which set of colours are the secondary colours?
questions.explain: Secondary colours (orange, green and purple) are made by mixing two primary colours together.

questions.q: Lino printing is an example of which printmaking process?
questions.explain: In relief printing, such as lino and woodcut, ink sits on the raised surface while the cut-away areas stay blank.

questions.q: In intaglio printing, such as etching, where is the ink that prints held?
options: In the lines incised below the surface of the plate
On the raised areas of the block
On a flat greasy drawing surface
questions.explain: Intaglio works in reverse to relief: ink is wiped into the sunken incised lines and the flat surface is wiped clean before printing.

questions.q: In a reduction lino print, the different colours are printed from...
options: A single block that is progressively cut away
A different block for each colour
A silk screen with paper stencils
questions.explain: In a reduction print one block is used throughout, being cut back further between each colour layer.

questions.q: A printmaker is printing a second colour over the first and needs the two layers to line up exactly. This alignment is achieved through...
questions.explain: Registration is the system of marks or guides used to position the paper and block so successive layers align accurately.

questions.q: An artist wants to produce a large edition of identical prints from a raised, carved design. Which process is most suitable?
options: Relief printing, such as lino or woodcut
questions.explain: Relief printing from a carved block allows many consistent impressions, whereas a monotype yields only a single print.

questions.q: Which tool is used to roll an even layer of ink onto a printing block?
questions.explain: A brayer, or roller, spreads a thin, even film of ink across the raised surface of a relief block.

questions.q: Carving stone or wood to make a sculpture is described as which kind of process?
questions.explain: Carving is subtractive because material is cut and removed to reveal the final form.

questions.q: Building up a figure from clay is described as an additive process because...
options: Material is added and built up to create the form
Material is removed from a solid block
A mould is used to reproduce the form
The finished piece is designed to move
questions.explain: Modelling is additive: soft material such as clay is gradually added and shaped to build the form.

questions.q: Why is an armature used when modelling in clay or wax?
options: It provides an internal support or framework for the material
It rolls ink evenly onto the surface
It adds colour to the finished surface
questions.explain: An armature is a rigid inner skeleton that supports and holds the shape of soft modelling material as it is built up.

questions.q: The lost-wax (cire perdue) process is used to...
options: Cast a metal sculpture from a wax original that is melted out
Carve a marble figure by removing stone
Print multiple colours from a single block
Weld found objects into an assemblage
questions.explain: In lost-wax casting a wax model is encased in a mould, then melted out so molten metal can fill the cavity it leaves.

questions.q: A sculptor deliberately shapes the empty spaces between and around the solid forms as part of the composition. These spaces are known as...
questions.explain: Negative space is the empty area around and between the solid (positive) forms and can be composed as deliberately as the forms themselves.

questions.q: A sculpture designed to be viewed from all sides is described as being...
questions.explain: A free-standing sculpture in the round is fully three-dimensional and can be viewed from every angle, unlike a relief attached to a background.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel GCSE Art & Design (1AD0) specification; Fine Art (Drawing, Painting, Printmaking, Sculpture)
